newsitem.title: INDIA: New Congress leader backs Indian premier.
newsitem.headline: New Congress leader backs Indian premier.

text.p: The new leader of India's Congress party reaffirmed his group's crucial support on Tuesday for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition.

Sitaram Kesri, 80, tapped on Monday to replace former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao as head of Congress, told reporters that the party would continue to offer make-or-break backing to the 13-party minority coalition.
"This is a decision taken under Narasimha Rao's leadership, and I agree we have to help all the forces fighting communalism," Kesri told a news conference.

He was referring to the alliance linking Congress and the United Front against the rightist Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which in general elections in April and May emerged as the single largest party in parliament.
The BJP held power for 11 days in May, but lacking an outright majority, had to step down in favour of the centre-left United Front, which had the outside backing of Congress.
Rao quit as party leader on Saturday after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a $100,000 criminal conspiracy case.
His abrupt departure sent shivers through the financial markets, which were concerned that turmoil in Congress might upset the ruling balance.
But Kesri's comments appeared to put those worries to rest and indicate he would pursue the policies of Rao, who as prime minister opened India's economy to foreign trade and investment.
"One can't distinguish me from Mr Rao," the United News of India quoted Kesri as saying.
Analysts said the change in Congress leaders was not expected to affect the new government's open-market economic policies, which have been welcomed by foreign investors.
Kesri said his priority would be to unify Congress, which has been hobbled by internal squabbling and splits.
He also pledged to battle corruption. "I will fight corruption whole heartedly," he said.

Seven of Rao's ministers quit earlier this year after being linked to a bribery scandal, and former communications minister Sukh Ram was arrested last week following the discovery of more than $1 million in cash in two of his homes.
The party's top decision-making body reached into the past to choose Kesri, a freedom fighter during the independence movement, as interim leader.

Kesri, who has served as Congress treasurer for 18 years, drew broad but not unequivocal support to take over the reins until the fractious party's plenary body meets to select a more permanent leader.

The date of that meeting has not been set, but it was agreed that the party should await the outcome of assembly elections in India's most populous state Uttar Pradesh, which start next Monday and end on October 7.
Kesri boasted the advantage of having links to Congress's heyday when it dominated the political stage. He also commands the confidence of Rao and his loyalists.
Asked what his first priority would be, Kesri said he would "carry on the message of Mahatma Gandhi to wipe out tears from the eyes of the downtrodden, the poor and the oppressed."
